seo_title: Hotel Property Insurance Claims: A Texas Owner Guide
meta_description: Hotel property insurance claims: what’s covered, common disputes, business income, documentation and appraisal for Texas hotels.
h1: Hotel Property Insurance Claims: How Texas Owners Protect Their Recovery
excerpt: Hotel property insurance claims involve rooms, systems, FF&E and lost income. Learn what is covered, why disputes happen, and how Texas hotel owners document claims.
key_takeaways: Hotel claims often combine building, FF&E, business income and extra expense coverages.
Per-room estimate errors multiply quickly across a property.
Document damage room by room, floor by floor and system by system.
Clean financial records drive a strong business income claim.
Appraisal can resolve disputes over scope, pricing and FF&E values.
body_html:
Hotel property insurance claims cover physical damage to a hotel's buildings, guest rooms, systems and contents, and often the lost income while rooms sit empty. They are more complex than most commercial claims because damage spreads across many identical rooms, building systems interact, and every day of closure costs revenue. Strong documentation and accurate estimates drive the outcome.

What do hotel property insurance claims cover?

A hotel's commercial property policy, often packaged with other coverages, typically responds to several categories of loss after a covered event:

  • Building: roofs, exterior walls, windows, structure, corridors, lobbies, guest rooms, pools and permanently installed equipment.
  • Business personal property: furniture, fixtures and equipment (FF&E) such as beds, case goods, televisions, linens, kitchen equipment and fitness equipment.
  • Business income: lost net income and continuing expenses while the hotel or part of it cannot operate.
  • Extra expense: reasonable costs to reduce downtime, such as temporary equipment, expedited shipping or relocating guests.
  • Additional coverages: debris removal, ordinance or law, spoilage, and sometimes utility service interruption, depending on the form.

Each of these categories may have its own limit, deductible, waiting period and documentation requirements. Reading the full policy, not just the summary, is the first step in any hotel claim.

Why hotel claims are more complex than other commercial claims

Hotels look like simple boxes from the outside, but claims on them are rarely simple.

Repetition multiplies small errors

A typical hotel has dozens or hundreds of nearly identical rooms. If an estimate misses one item per room, such as a wall covering, a vanity top or a PTAC unit, the error is multiplied across every affected room. A small per-room gap can become a large claim gap.

Building systems are interconnected

Central HVAC, fire sprinklers, alarm systems, elevators, kitchens and laundry facilities all tie together. Damage in one area, such as a roof leak over a mechanical room, can disrupt operations far beyond the visible damage.

Brand standards affect repairs

Franchised hotels often must meet brand standards for finishes, FF&E and guest-facing areas. That can create disputes over whether replacement materials of "like kind and quality" must also satisfy brand requirements, and over matching when only some rooms or floors were damaged.

Revenue loss is immediate

Unlike an office building with long-term leases, a hotel loses revenue the first night a room is out of service. Business income claims start right away and depend on accurate records.

Common causes of hotel property damage in Texas

Texas hotels face a wide range of weather and building risks. The most common sources of claims include:

Cause of lossTypical damageWhere it is most common in Texas
HailRoof membranes, rooftop HVAC units, skylights, exterior finishes, signageDallas–Fort Worth, Central Texas, Panhandle, West Texas
Hurricane and tropical storm windRoof systems, windows, balconies, wind-driven rain intrusion into roomsHouston, Galveston, Corpus Christi, Beaumont
Freeze eventsBurst sprinkler and domestic water lines, flooded floors, damaged drywall and FF&EStatewide, especially in buildings not designed for extended freezes
Plumbing failuresWater migration through multiple floors and roomsStatewide
Fire and smokeStructural damage, smoke and soot throughout corridors and HVACStatewide

Flood is usually excluded from standard property policies and covered, if at all, by separate flood insurance. That distinction matters a great deal for coastal properties. Hotel owners near the Galveston coast should know exactly which policy covers wind, which covers flood, and what their named-storm deductible is.

Common disputes in hotel property insurance claims

Most disputes in hotel property insurance claims are about how much the loss is worth, not whether it happened. The issues we see most often include:

  • Room count and scope. The carrier counts fewer affected rooms than the hotel's own inspection found, or limits repairs to visible stains rather than the full extent of moisture.
  • Roof repair versus replacement. Hail-damaged membranes, coatings and rooftop equipment are spot repaired on paper when the system needs replacement. See commercial roof hail damage claims.
  • Matching and uniformity. Replacing carpet or wall coverings in some rooms but not adjacent corridors can leave a property out of brand standard. Our guide to matching issues in insurance claims covers this in more detail.
  • FF&E valuation. Depreciation on furniture and equipment, and whether contaminated items can be cleaned or must be replaced.
  • Pricing. Unit costs that do not reflect hospitality-grade materials or the real cost of phased work in an operating hotel.
  • Business income calculations. Disagreements over occupancy projections, average daily rate, seasonality and the length of the restoration period.

Business income and hotel claims

For many hotels, the business income portion of the claim rivals the physical damage. It usually covers lost net income plus continuing normal operating expenses during the period of restoration, subject to a waiting period and the policy's terms.

Strong business income claims rely on clean financial records:

  1. Monthly profit and loss statements for at least the prior two to three years
  2. Occupancy, average daily rate and revenue per available room reports
  3. Advance bookings, group contracts and cancellations tied to the loss
  4. Payroll records, especially for staff retained during closure
  5. Records of extra expenses incurred to reopen sooner

Business income and property damage claims are linked: a longer repair timeline extends the income loss. Our article on business interruption vs property damage claims explains how the two interact.

Tip: Take guest rooms out of inventory in your property management system with a note tying each room to the loss. That creates a contemporaneous, date-stamped record of exactly which rooms were unavailable and for how long.

How to document a hotel insurance claim

Documentation in a hotel claim needs to be organized by room, floor and system. The goal is to let anyone reviewing the file, whether an adjuster, appraiser or umpire, understand the damage without visiting every room.

  • Room-by-room log: list every affected room with photos, moisture readings and a short description of damage.
  • Common area documentation: lobbies, corridors, stairwells, meeting rooms, kitchens, pools and back-of-house areas.
  • Roof and exterior: drone imagery, close-up photos of hail impacts or wind damage, and documentation of rooftop equipment.
  • FF&E inventory: quantities, models, purchase dates and condition before the loss.
  • Mitigation records: drying logs, moisture maps, invoices and photos from restoration contractors.
  • 3D scans: Matterport 3D documentation captures entire floors, accurate measurements and conditions before demolition begins.

Our free claim documentation checklist can help your management team build a complete file quickly.

How long do hotel property insurance claims take?

There is no standard timeline. A contained plumbing loss affecting a handful of rooms may resolve in weeks. A hurricane or hail claim affecting the roof, dozens of rooms and the business income line can take many months, especially if the carrier hires engineers and accountants.

Texas law sets the pace for parts of the process. Under the prompt payment rules in chapter 542, carriers generally must acknowledge the claim within 15 days, accept or reject it within 15 business days after receiving the information they requested (with extensions up to 45 days), and pay within 5 business days after accepting. Those deadlines can restart as new information is requested, so keep a written log of every request and response.

Ways to keep a hotel claim moving

  1. Name one point of contact at the property who owns all claim communication.
  2. Respond to document requests in writing, quickly and completely.
  3. Ask for partial payments on undisputed amounts so repairs can start.
  4. Schedule re-inspections promptly when hidden damage is uncovered during demolition.
  5. Track the reopening date for each room block so business income can be calculated accurately.

Partial payments matter more for hotels than for most properties. Every week of delay extends the period of restoration, and with it the business income loss both sides are trying to measure.

Using appraisal to resolve hotel claim disputes

When the hotel and the carrier agree there was a covered loss but disagree on its value, the policy's appraisal clause offers a structured way to resolve it. Each side names an independent appraiser, the appraisers try to agree on the amount of loss, and an umpire decides anything they cannot agree on. An award signed by any two of the three sets the amount.

Appraisal fits hotel claims well because the disputes tend to be technical: room counts, repair methods, pricing and FF&E values. Under Texas law, appraisers decide the amount of loss and may weigh causation and the extent of damage, but they do not decide coverage. For very large hotel claims, see our guide to large loss insurance appraisal in Texas.

Keep in mind Texas Insurance Code chapter 542 deadlines for acknowledging, deciding and paying claims continue to matter, and weather-related claims generally require 61 days' notice before suit under chapter 542A. This is general information, not legal advice.

Mistakes hotel owners should avoid

  • Delaying mitigation. Water damage spreads quickly through a multi-story building. Most policies require reasonable steps to prevent further damage.
  • Discarding damaged FF&E too early. Photograph, inventory and, where practical, retain samples before disposal.
  • Accepting a sample-based scope. If the carrier inspected a few rooms and extrapolated, make sure every affected room is actually accounted for.
  • Ignoring brand requirements. Share franchise standards with the adjuster early when they affect materials or matching.
  • Letting the business income claim lag. Gather financial records at the start rather than months later.

faqs.q: Does hotel insurance cover lost revenue after a storm?
faqs.a: Many hotel policies include business income coverage that pays lost net income and continuing expenses while the property cannot operate because of covered physical damage. Coverage usually starts after a waiting period and lasts through the period of restoration. Check your policy for limits, waiting periods and any extended period of indemnity.

faqs.q: How do insurers handle damage across many identical hotel rooms?
faqs.a: Adjusters often inspect a sample of rooms and extrapolate. That can miss damage in rooms that were not inspected. Hotel owners should keep a room-by-room log with photos and moisture readings so every affected room is accounted for in the estimate, not just the ones the adjuster visited.

faqs.q: Are hotel brand standards covered in an insurance claim?
faqs.a: Policies generally pay for materials of like kind and quality, which may or may not satisfy franchise requirements. Disputes can arise when replacements in some rooms no longer match others. Share brand standards with the adjuster early and document why specific materials or uniform replacement are reasonable for the property.

faqs.q: Can a hotel use appraisal for a business income dispute?
faqs.a: Often, yes, when the parties disagree on the amount of the income loss rather than on coverage. Business income appraisals depend on financial records such as occupancy, average daily rate and profit and loss statements. Policy language varies, so confirm that your appraisal clause applies to the disputed coverage.

faqs.q: What should a hotel do first after water or storm damage?
faqs.a: Protect guests and staff, stop the source of damage, and start mitigation such as water extraction and drying. Then notify the carrier, photograph everything before cleanup, take affected rooms out of inventory with notes tying them to the loss, and keep every invoice for emergency work and extra expenses.
